title: Optimising areas and lengths under constraints
transcript: An optimisation problem asks for the greatest or least possible result under a rule. First use the rule to express the possibilities in terms of one choice. Many rectangle problems reward balance. Show why the nearby legal sizes give the best area.

AMC practice may ask for the largest area or smallest required boundary. Write which quantity stays fixed. A Rossmoyne style question may require whole-number dimensions or one side against a wall. Give a reason that every other choice is worse.
A rectangle has perimeter twenty-six metres and width four metres. What is its area? Use half of the perimeter to find one width plus one length.
The perimeter has two copies of each side. Half is thirteen, so the length is thirteen minus four, which is nine. Multiply width by length. The area is thirty-six square metres.
A rectangle with whole-number side lengths has perimeter twenty-six. What is the greatest possible area? Compare side lengths close to each other with ones far apart.

If the longer side exceeds the shorter by at least two, moving one unit from the longer to the shorter makes their product larger. The sum of the sides stays fixed. The closest pair has lengths six and seven. The greatest area is forty-two square units.

Build a rectangular pen against a wall using exactly forty-five metres of fencing. Fence only the other three sides, and use whole-number lengths. Find the largest area and the dimensions that give it.

If x is a side going out from the wall, there are two such sides. The remaining fenced side measures forty-five minus twice x. Area is half the product of twice x and the remaining length. Those two factors have a fixed sum, so the best factors are as close together as possible. Twice x must be even. Check the even values closest to half of forty-five.

The best width is eleven metres, giving an area of two hundred and fifty-three square metres. Any other candidate makes the two factors farther apart. The larger gap reduces their product, so no farther candidate can beat this result.

A side against a wall does not use fencing. Count only the two widths and the fenced length before writing the equation. The best real-number answer can break an integer rule. Compare the nearby whole-number possibilities around that balance point.

Write the fixed sum, boundary or budget. Reduce the possible outcomes to one variable. Show that moving towards balance increases the product until you reach the closest legal dimensions. Check any ties.
